lead: An ophthalmic instrument measures one property of the eye with a calibrated optical or mechanical method. A tonometer measures intra-ocular pressure, the fluid pressure inside the eye. A slit lamp builds a bright optical section so a clinician can see cornea, anterior chamber and lens layer by layer. An auto refractometer measures the lens power needed to focus the eye. These three measurements support glaucoma screening, eye examination and spectacle prescription in every eye clinic.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.4 for patient-safe low-current design, and basic lens optics (focal length, dioptre) from first-year physics.

sections.h3: Tonometry: pressure from force and area

blocks.text: Intra-ocular pressure (IOP) is the pressure of the aqueous humour inside the eyeball. It is measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg). Normal is about 10 to 21 mmHg. High pressure damages the optic nerve in glaucoma, so tonometry is a screening test.

Indentation tonometry uses a Schiotz tonometer. A known weight pushes a plunger into the cornea. The scale reading is not pressure directly; a conversion table for that weight and instrument gives mmHg. Corneal stiffness affects the reading, so the table is a calibration, not a pure physics answer.

blocks.where: P is pressure in pascals (Pa); F is force in newtons (N); A is flattened area in square metres (m²).

blocks.text: A Goldmann tonometer uses a prism on the slit lamp. The prism flattens a circle of diameter 3.06 mm, so A = π(1.53 mm)² = 7.35 mm². The clinician puts one drop of local anaesthetic and fluorescein in the eye. Under blue light the tear film is stained, and two green arcs show the flattened circle. The force knob is turned until the arcs just touch. Force in millinewtons (mN) divided by this fixed area gives pressure; the prism scale is marked in mmHg.

Non-contact tonometry uses a short air puff. The puff flattens the cornea and an optical detector times the flattening. It needs no drop and no contact, so it suits screening. It is less reliable with an irregular cornea.
Calibration checks: zero the instrument, check the prism or probe, and test against a known calibration verifier. A drifted tonometer gives a wrong glaucoma decision.

sections.h3: Slit lamp: an optical section of the eye

blocks.text: The slit lamp is a biomicroscope: a microscope and a lamp on one movable base. The lamp arm carries a bright source and an adjustable slit aperture. The microscope arm carries the objective and eyepieces. A joystick moves the instrument in x, y and z. The patient rests chin and forehead on supports.

With wide diffuse light you scan lids, conjunctiva, cornea, iris and lens. With a narrow slit at an angle you get an optic section: a thin illuminated slice through transparent tissue. The cornea appears as a curved band, the anterior chamber as dark space, and the lens shows layers. Moving the slit shows depth, thickness, deposits and cells.

The slit lamp is a platform, not one test. With a gonioscopy lens it views the drainage angle; with a fundus lens it gives a magnified view of the retina and optic disc. Those lenses belong to ophthalmology courses. The main safety point is light exposure and patient comfort; the instrument is non-contact except for the lens.

Refraction is the lens power that corrects a focus error. It is written as sphere, cylinder and axis. Sphere (S) is spherical power in dioptres (D), positive for hyperopia and negative for myopia. Cylinder (C) is astigmatic power. Axis is the meridian in degrees from 0 to 180.

An auto refractometer projects an infra-red target into the eye. Infra-red is invisible and keeps the pupil wide. Light reflects from the retina and passes back through the eye's optics. A Shack-Hartmann sensor uses a lenslet array: each small lens makes a spot. A perfect eye gives a regular grid; a defocused or astigmatic eye shifts the spots. The computer fits these shifts to sphere, cylinder and axis. Some instruments use a knife-edge or a moving pattern instead.

The result is objective. The patient then reads a chart for visual acuity, which is sharpness, not refraction. A person can have 6/6 acuity with glasses and still need a strong prescription. The clinician fine-tunes the auto refractometer reading by subjective refraction.
Uses: busy clinics, screening camps, before cataract surgery, and children who cannot cooperate with a manual test. Calibration uses a model eye of known power.

spec.title: Applanation tonometry
spec.aria: Four-step chain of applanation tonometry: tear film, prism flattening a 3.06 mm circle, force knob, then pressure by P = F/A.

examples.question: A Goldmann prism flattens a circle of diameter 3.06 mm when the force knob is set to 20 mN. Find the intra-ocular pressure in mmHg.
steps: Diameter d = 3.06 mm, so radius r = d/2 = 1.53 mm.
Area A = πr² = π × (1.53 mm)² = 7.35 mm² = 7.35 × 10⁻⁶ m².
examples.answer: The intra-ocular pressure is 20.4 mmHg, inside the normal range of about 10 to 21 mmHg.
examples.check:
import math
d_mm = 3.06
r_mm = d_mm / 2
area_mm2 = math.pi * r_mm ** 2
area_m2 = area_mm2 * 1e-6
force_mN = 20
force_N = force_mN * 1e-3
pressure_Pa = force_N / area_m2
pressure_mmHg = pressure_Pa / 133.3
print(round(pressure_mmHg, 1))

traps: mmHg is not Pa: 1 mmHg = 133.3 Pa. Convert before comparing with a pascal answer, and keep mN to N straight (20 mN = 0.020 N).
Imbert-Fick assumes a thin, dry, flexible cornea. The tear film pulls the prism in, so the Goldmann design fixes the area and relies on prism calibration.
A Schiotz scale reading is not mmHg. The conversion table depends on the weight used and the instrument.
Refraction is not visual acuity. A 6/6 eye with glasses can still have a -2.00 D prescription.
The slit lamp is not a tonometer. It is a viewing platform; pressure comes from a tonometer, often mounted on it.

quiz.q: State the normal intra-ocular pressure range and its unit.
Why does a Goldmann tonometer keep the flattened diameter fixed at 3.06 mm?
quiz.a: Imbert-Fick P = F/A needs a known area. A fixed area lets the force knob be marked directly in mmHg and reduces errors from variable contact. The tear film and corneal stiffness also make a fixed, calibrated geometry necessary.

quiz.q: A Goldmann prism flattens the standard 3.06 mm circle with a force of 15 mN. Find the pressure in mmHg.
Why is a Schiotz scale reading converted through a table instead of using P = F/A directly?
quiz.a: The plunger indents a curved, stiff cornea; the load is not spread over a simple flat area, and corneal resistance adds to fluid pressure. The table is an empirical calibration for a given weight and instrument.

quiz.q: Name the main parts of a slit lamp and one thing an optic section shows.
quiz.a: Lamp arm with slit aperture, biomicroscope with objective and eyepieces, joystick and patient support. An optic section shows depth and layers of cornea or lens.

quiz.q: An auto refractometer reads -2.00 DS / -0.75 DC × 180. What do the three numbers mean?
quiz.a: Sphere -2.00 D corrects myopia. Cylinder -0.75 D corrects astigmatism. Axis 180° gives the meridian of the cylinder.

quiz.q: Why does an auto refractometer use infra-red light, and why is its result not the same as visual acuity?
quiz.a: Infra-red is invisible, so it does not stimulate the pupil reflex strongly and is comfortable; it measures the optical wavefront. Visual acuity is a behavioural measure of the smallest detail seen, so it depends on neural and subjective factors as well.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one limitation of non-contact air-puff tonometry.
quiz.a: Advantage: no anaesthetic drop and no contact, so quick screening. Limitation: less reliable with an irregular cornea or after corneal surgery.

beyond: Not for the exam. Dynamic contour tonometry and corneal hysteresis try to remove corneal stiffness from pressure measurement. Wavefront aberrometers map higher-order aberrations beyond sphere and cylinder. Search next for 'ocular response analyser', 'Shack-Hartmann aberrometer' and 'non-contact tonometry'. These are active areas in optometry and ophthalmology.
